confidence_why: Kilpatrick's 1985 phonology and the 2018 SIL South Sudan grammar, dictionary and consonant-and-vowel books by Moi and colleagues with Stirtz both describe Bongo as a tone language with lexical tone contrasts on nouns and verbs and neither gives any word-stress rule, so the tonal reading has no rival, though only two independent descriptions exist and Kilpatrick's single passing mention of stressed syllables leaves stress placement undescribed.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Bongo has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; Kilpatrick adds that the language is tonal (two phonemic tones) and that stress, if present, has no stated placement - compatible with the empty record, so 'refines'. Both quoted passages were verified against two independent scans (Rosetta djvu text and tesseract scanned of the OPSL 4 facsimile), which agree word for word. The live sil.org returned the an automated-access block on both attempts
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bongo is a two-tone language (phonemic H and L; phonetic mid is an allotone of L after H; falling tone only on long vowels or vowel clusters), with lexical tone contrasts on every syllable of mono-, di- and trisyllabic words. The paper has no stress section and gives no rule for where stress falls; its single mention says only that vowels of 'stressed syllables' are slightly lengthened and that the peak syllable of an utterance is lengthened as an intonational feature. Sec. 6.4 treats intonation at the sentence level (yes-no questions rising, statements and WH-questions falling). The TOC (pp. 1-2) lists no stress/accent heading, and pp. 50-62 (word list, notes, references) contain nothing on stress. The author flags 'prosodic features' as needing more investigation (p. 3).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only stress-related remark is the phonetic lengthening of stressed-syllable vowels (p. 33)
new_statements.identity_note: Kilpatrick 1985 describes the Tonj dialect (data gathered at Tonj from Gu Ba Kpuyu with Lynne Callinan, 1970s; note 6 records Bussere /r/ vs Tonj /l/ correspondences). Santandrea 1963, per Kilpatrick p. 3, bases its phonological summary on the Bussere dialect (the Wau-road community). Both are Bongo [bot] = bong1285.

Paper presented at the 26th International Conference on Historical Linguistics (ICHL26), Heidelberg, September 2023. (HAL halshs-04366808, abstract only.)
tone_statements.quote: Bongo, Jur Mödö and Morokodo have all chosen the umlaut or two dots over a letter to indicate at least some of their [+ATR] vowels. ... The reason for Baka avoiding diacritics over letters is that it was decided to mark tone in that language. There are two contrasting tones and all high tones are indicated by an acute accent over the vowel. ... For the other three languages, although they all have two-tone systems similar to Baka, it was concluded that there was no need to indicate tone in the orthography and that context was adequate to decide the meaning in all but a few cases.
tone_statements.summary: Group overview: Bongo has a 'two-tone system similar to Baka' (two contrasting tones, high marked in Baka); tone not written in Bongo orthography. Labels/TBU (two level tones, one per syllable) given only for Jur Mödö, p. 80; 'level' for Bongo is by analogy. No Bongo tone-marked forms; no stress.

tone_statements.quote: Le système *SBB, commun à l'ensemble des langues sara-bongo-baguirmiennes, se subdivise en trois branches respectivement représentées par le groupe modo-'beli-baka, le bongo (langue unique) et l'ensemble des autres langues, dites 'occidentales'. Le système *OCC, commun à ces dernières et notamment caractérisé par le développement d'un troisième registre tonal, se subdivise à son tour en cinq rameaux [...] Les correspondances tonales nominales conduisent à l'identification de six formules originelles, soit *11/*12/*21a/*21b/*21c/*22, qui ne correspondent vraisemblablement qu'à cinq schèmes réellement distinctifs dans un sytème originel *SBB à deux registres
tone_statements.translation: The *SBB system, common to all the Sara-Bongo-Bagirmi languages, divides into three branches represented respectively by the Modo-'Beli-Baka group, Bongo (a single language) and all the other, so-called 'western', languages. The *OCC system, common to the latter and characterised notably by the development of a third tone register, divides in turn into five sub-branches [...] The nominal tone correspondences lead to the identification of six original formulae, *11/*12/*21a/*21b/*21c/*22, which probably correspond to only five really distinctive patterns in an original two-register *SBB system
tone_statements.summary: Bongo treated as a two-register (H/L) language continuing the proto-SBB two-tone system; no third register.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress between the sources: only Kilpatrick 1985 could be opened, and it gives no placement rule. On tone there is a reported disagreement: Kilpatrick posits two phonemic tones (H, L; mid = allotone of L after H), while her note 12 (p. 61) says Santandrea 'posits three phonemic tones based on a single contrast', a contrast she could not replicate ('we could only elicit /hetira/ for body, and recorded different vowels for the other two words'). Santandrea's own text could not be opened (in copyright, HathiTrust search-only, no open copy anywhere found).

(2) The deciding source is a dedicated descriptive phonology (62 pp) with a full tone chapter; it is the primary phonology in Glottolog's list (the 1979 entry is its unpublished draft). sources.note: Presentation, sections 'Classification, genealogie et histoire des langues' and 'Correspondances > Formules tonales': the *SBB proto-system common to all SBB languages had two registers (nominal formulae *11/*12/*21a/*21b/*21c/*22, verb classes *A-*D2); the third register is an innovation of the *OCC ('western') node, from which Bongo (a primary branch of its own) is excluded, so Bongo reflexes are coded in the two-register scheme (1 = B, 2 = H); every Bongo form in the database is tone-marked from Nougayrol's unpublished Lexique bongo.

tone.quote: Some noteworthy linguistic features about Bongo include implosives, labiovelar affricates, ten vowel phonemes (5 [+ATR] and 5 [-ATR]), three syllable types (V, CV, CVC), vowel harmony (in which [-ATR] vowels tend to change to [+ATR]), four phonetic tones, and two phonemic tones (Kilpatrick 1985). However, according to Daniel Rabbi, tone is often not used in day-to-day speech (personal communication, November 11, 2012).

tone.quote: ... correspondances phoniques régulières touchant les consonnes, les voyelles et les tons ... – la formule tonale *BH (bas-haut) est représentée par BH en modo, par (B)H en bongo, par BM (bas-moyen) en yulu, ndoka et sar et par MM (moyen-moyen) en gula mere. ... Le passage de deux à trois hauteurs tonales distinctives (et les correspondances qui en résultent dans le domaine de la morphologie verbale) caractérise notamment la branche des langues ‘occidentales’ (*OCC), qui s’est solidairement détachée des autres langues avant de se diversifier à son tour.
tone.locator: sections 2 'Parenté des langues SBB' and 3 'Filiation des langues SBB', manuscript pp. 1-2; tone definition in note 1, p. 1; Bongo forms in Tableau 2, p. 8
tone.translation: ... regular sound correspondences involving consonants, vowels and tones ... - the tonal formula *BH (low-high) is represented by BH in Modo, by (B)H in Bongo, by BM (low-mid) in Yulu, Ndoka and Sar and by MM (mid-mid) in Gula Mere. ... The passage from two to three distinctive tone heights (and the resulting correspondences in verbal morphology) characterises in particular the branch of the 'western' languages (*OCC), which split off from the other languages as a block before diversifying in turn.
tone.summary: Comparative-historical paper: tones are pitch heights on syllables (note 1, Yulu examples); Bongo reflex of *low-high is (low)-high; three heights are a western-branch innovation, so two for Bongo is implied, not stated as an inventory. Stress: nil.
